PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

### OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
### PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
## TAX TO FUND EDUCATION AND EARLY CHILDHOOD PROGRAMS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
- Increases personal income tax rates on annual earnings over $7,316 using sliding scale from .4% for lowest individual earners to 2.2% for individuals earning over $2.5 million, for twelve years.
- During first four years, allocates 60% of revenues to K–12 schools, 30% to repaying state debt, and 10% to early childhood programs.
Thereafter, allocates 85% of revenues to K–12 schools, 15% to early childhood programs.
- Provides K–12 funds on school-specific, per-pupil basis, subject to local control, audits, and public input.
- Prohibits state from directing new funds.
### Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact:
- Increase in state personal income tax revenues from 2013 through 2024.
The increase would be roughly $10 billion in 2013–14, tending to increase over time.

This measure raises personal income taxes on most

The revenues raised by this tax increase would be spent on public schools, child care and preschool programs, and state debt payments.

Increases PIT Rates.
This measure increases state PIT rates on all but the lowest income bracket, effective over the 12-year period from 2013 through 2024.
As shown in Figure 1, the additional marginal tax rates would increase with each higher tax bracket.

## Summary
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants.
**Fiscal Impact:** Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.
**Supporters:** Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA **Opponents:** Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.

## Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
## No
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

## TAX TO FUND EDUCATION AND EARLY CHILDHOOD PROGRAMS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
- Increases personal income tax rates on annual earnings over $7,316 using sliding scale from .4% for lowest individual earners to 2.2% for individuals earning over $2.5 million, for twelve years.
- During first four years, allocates 60% of revenues to K–12 schools, 30% to repaying state debt, and 10% to early childhood programs.
Thereafter, allocates 85% of revenues to K–12 schools, 15% to early childhood programs.
- Provides K–12 funds on school-specific, per-pupil basis, subject to local control, audits, and public input.
- Prohibits state from directing new funds.

- Increase in state personal income tax revenues from 2013 through 2024.

Increases PIT Rates.

As shown in Figure 1, the additional marginal tax rates would increase with each higher tax bracket.

ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi-
Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic
research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge
about how the human body works. The next stage is
applied and clinical research, which aims to develop
and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities
do most of the basic research, while companies do
most of the applied and clinical research. The third
R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments
to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new
treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients.
Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these
stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding
for medical R&D in the United States totaled about
$300 billion in 2023. Companies and government
agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health)
are the major funding sources for R&D nationally
and in California. Beyond these funding sources,
California voters have approved two ballot measures—
Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)—
giving the state authority to issue general obligation

bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined,
the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion
in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for
the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest
over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid
from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the
account the state uses to pay for most public services,
including education, health care, and prisons.) For
more information about bonds, see “Overview of State
Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research.
Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion
general obligation bond for research in immunology
and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the
body’s immune system and how it protects the body
from abnormal cells and other causes of disease.
Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the
immune system fight diseases more effectively. The
measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond
funds be used for immunology research on cancer,

ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state
administrative costs. Payments on the bond would
come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond
funds would go to a research institute specializing
in immunology and immunotherapy. The California
Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select
the institute. The selected institute must meet several
criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding,
and collaboration with a University of California (UC)
campus. The institute would use the bond funds for
research. Each year, the institute must issue a public
report on its activities and have an independent
financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out
the other half of bond funds as competitive research
grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy.
The council would consist of representatives from
7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and
nonprofit research institutions in California. The council
would set research priorities and select grant recipients
from among its member organizations. Similar to the
institute, the council would have public reporting and
audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries
First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38
requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH,
try to generate the most revenue possible from the
funded research. (Research, for example, could lead
to the development of a new medical treatment.)
Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given
to the state. This revenue must first go into the state
General Fund until it repays the cost of the research
bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest).
Any additional revenue would be used for future
immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
• Requires Purchases From California Suppliers.
Grant recipients must buy at least half of their
goods and services from California suppliers
when reasonably possible.
• Requires California Patient Discount. Any
treatment developed through funded research
and sold in California must generally be offered at
a 20 percent discount.
C O N T I N U E D
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million
Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The
state General Fund cost to repay the bond would
be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
20 years. The annual cost would be about one-quarter
of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General
Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the
money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be
about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation)
than if the state paid up-front with money it already
has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries.
The state could receive revenue from research funded
by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain
but could be significant. It would depend on how many
research projects lead to marketable treatments and
how much money any given treatment generates. The
timing of these revenues and how long it would take to
offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could
take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely
would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly
on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal,
which pays for health care for low-income Californians).
For example, if the funded research leads to new
medical treatments, the average cost of patient care
could either increase or decrease. As a result, the
overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

★ ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38 ★
California recognizes that continued investment in science is
essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that
goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state
borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research
through a new University of California institute. Although the
objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are
flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives
to direct research funding toward selected topics. California
has already created separate funding programs for stem cell
research and precision medicine. This measure would add
another highly focused program. Research priorities should
be established through scientific review and public health
planning—not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s
disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental
illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions.
Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather
than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific
research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the
bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to
$500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds
are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived
infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is
different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve
patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never
produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will
generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities
rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded
research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies
typically invest the far greater resources required for product
development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory
approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not
flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with
state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While
this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to
prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices
are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research.
But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally
responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based
on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and
public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures
financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott
Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency
modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National
Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific
areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities
through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as
new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not
advanced, it received support from the University of California,
the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians
and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the
future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient
financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting
research priorities. California can and should support medical
research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan, Ph.D.

California voters will decide in November whether Proposition (Prop) 38 should authorize substantial state funding for immunology and immunotherapy research.
The initiative would fund immunology and immunotherapy research aimed at harnessing the body’s immune system to develop new treatments, medical procedures and potential cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.

At least half of the bond proceeds, or $4.2 billion, would be dedicated exclusively to research.
Additionally, Prop 38 would make it mandatory for the state to enter into an agreement with a qualified nonprofit institute focused and dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the initiative’s effective date.
The research institute must be affiliated with the University of California.
The third component mandates that the remaining bond revenue must be directed to California-based public and nonprofit medical institutions through a peer-reviewed grant process.

Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these
stages.

★ ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38 ★
California recognizes that continued investment in science is
essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that
goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state
borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research
through a new University of California institute. Although the
objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are
flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives
to direct research funding toward selected topics. California
has already created separate funding programs for stem cell
research and precision medicine. This measure would add
another highly focused program. Research priorities should
be established through scientific review and public health
planning—not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s
disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental
illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions.
Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather
than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific
research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the
bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to
$500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds
are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived
infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is
different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve
patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never
produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will
generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities
rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded
research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies
typically invest the far greater resources required for product
development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory
approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not
flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with
state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While
this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to
prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices
are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research.
But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally
responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based
on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and
public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures
financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott
Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency
modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National
Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific
areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities
through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as
new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not
advanced, it received support from the University of California,
the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians
and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the
future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient
financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting
research priorities. California can and should support medical
research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan, Ph.D.

BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi-
Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic
research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge
about how the human body works. The next stage is
applied and clinical research, which aims to develop
and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities
do most of the basic research, while companies do
most of the applied and clinical research. The third
R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments
to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new
treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients.
Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these
stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding
for medical R&D in the United States totaled about
$300 billion in 2023. Companies and government
agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health)
are the major funding sources for R&D nationally
and in California. Beyond these funding sources,
California voters have approved two ballot measures—
Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)—
giving the state authority to issue general obligation

Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond
funds would go to a research institute specializing
in immunology and immunotherapy. The California
Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select
the institute. The selected institute must meet several
criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding,
and collaboration with a University of California (UC)
campus. The institute would use the bond funds for
research. Each year, the institute must issue a public
report on its activities and have an independent
financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out
the other half of bond funds as competitive research
grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy.
The council would consist of representatives from
7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and
nonprofit research institutions in California. The council
would set research priorities and select grant recipients
from among its member organizations. Similar to the
institute, the council would have public reporting and
audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries
First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38
requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH,
try to generate the most revenue possible from the
funded research. (Research, for example, could lead
to the development of a new medical treatment.)
Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given
to the state. This revenue must first go into the state
General Fund until it repays the cost of the research
bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest).
Any additional revenue would be used for future
immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
• Requires Purchases From California Suppliers.
Grant recipients must buy at least half of their
goods and services from California suppliers
when reasonably possible.
• Requires California Patient Discount. Any
treatment developed through funded research
and sold in California must generally be offered at
a 20 percent discount.
C O N T I N U E D
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million
Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The
state General Fund cost to repay the bond would
be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
20 years. The annual cost would be about one-quarter
of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General
Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the
money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be
about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation)
than if the state paid up-front with money it already
has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries.
The state could receive revenue from research funded
by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain
but could be significant. It would depend on how many
research projects lead to marketable treatments and
how much money any given treatment generates. The
timing of these revenues and how long it would take to
offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could
take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely
would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly
on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal,
which pays for health care for low-income Californians).
For example, if the funded research leads to new
medical treatments, the average cost of patient care
could either increase or decrease. As a result, the
overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

# On your November ballot: Prop 38
California voters will decide in November whether Proposition (Prop) 38 should authorize substantial state funding for immunology and immunotherapy research.
The initiative would fund immunology and immunotherapy research aimed at harnessing the body’s immune system to develop new treatments, medical procedures and potential cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.

First, the initiative would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to support immunology and immunotherapy research.
At least half of the bond proceeds, or $4.2 billion, would be dedicated exclusively to research.
Additionally, Prop 38 would make it mandatory for the state to enter into an agreement with a qualified nonprofit institute focused and dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the initiative’s effective date.
The research institute must be affiliated with the University of California.
The third component mandates that the remaining bond revenue must be directed to California-based public and nonprofit medical institutions through a peer-reviewed grant process.
California would borrow the $8.4 billion with issues of bonds and would repay the debt over time with interest.

BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi-
Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic
research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge
about how the human body works. The next stage is
applied and clinical research, which aims to develop
and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities
do most of the basic research, while companies do
most of the applied and clinical research. The third
R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments
to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new
treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients.
Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these
stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding
for medical R&D in the United States totaled about
$300 billion in 2023. Companies and government
agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health)
are the major funding sources for R&D nationally
and in California. Beyond these funding sources,
California voters have approved two ballot measures—
Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)—
giving the state authority to issue general obligation

Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond
funds would go to a research institute specializing
in immunology and immunotherapy. The California
Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select
the institute. The selected institute must meet several
criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding,
and collaboration with a University of California (UC)
campus. The institute would use the bond funds for
research. Each year, the institute must issue a public
report on its activities and have an independent
financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out
the other half of bond funds as competitive research
grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy.
The council would consist of representatives from
7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and
nonprofit research institutions in California. The council
would set research priorities and select grant recipients
from among its member organizations. Similar to the
institute, the council would have public reporting and
audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries
First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38
requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH,
try to generate the most revenue possible from the
funded research. (Research, for example, could lead
to the development of a new medical treatment.)
Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given
to the state. This revenue must first go into the state
General Fund until it repays the cost of the research
bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest).
Any additional revenue would be used for future
immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
• Requires Purchases From California Suppliers.
Grant recipients must buy at least half of their
goods and services from California suppliers
when reasonably possible.
• Requires California Patient Discount. Any
treatment developed through funded research
and sold in California must generally be offered at
a 20 percent discount.
C O N T I N U E D
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million
Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The
state General Fund cost to repay the bond would
be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
20 years. The annual cost would be about one-quarter
of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General
Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the
money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be
about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation)
than if the state paid up-front with money it already
has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries.
The state could receive revenue from research funded
by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain
but could be significant. It would depend on how many
research projects lead to marketable treatments and
how much money any given treatment generates. The
timing of these revenues and how long it would take to
offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could
take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely
would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly
on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal,
which pays for health care for low-income Californians).
For example, if the funded research leads to new
medical treatments, the average cost of patient care
could either increase or decrease. As a result, the
overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

★ ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38 ★
California recognizes that continued investment in science is
essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that
goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state
borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research
through a new University of California institute. Although the
objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are
flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives
to direct research funding toward selected topics. California
has already created separate funding programs for stem cell
research and precision medicine. This measure would add
another highly focused program. Research priorities should
be established through scientific review and public health
planning—not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s
disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental
illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions.
Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather
than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific
research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the
bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to
$500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds
are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived
infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is
different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve
patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never
produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will
generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities
rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded
research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies
typically invest the far greater resources required for product
development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory
approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not
flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with
state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While
this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to
prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices
are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research.
But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally
responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based
on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and
public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures
financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott
Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency
modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National
Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific
areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities
through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as
new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not
advanced, it received support from the University of California,
the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians
and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the
future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient
financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting
research priorities. California can and should support medical
research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

### Proposition 38: NO
Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund research into treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and other diseases that can be fought through immunotherapy.
It would also require the drugs developed through this research to be sold at discounted rates.
At face value, this proposition seems reasonable.
However, a deeper look into Prop.
38 shows us that it is rife with issues.
CalMatters found that about 50% of the funding sourced from Prop.
38 is likely to go to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy — a nonprofit that had three employees as of last month.
It is unclear whether this institute has the capacity to handle billions of dollars.
Further, the writer of the proposition, Gary K. Michelson, is the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy’s primary funder.
While we acknowledge the pressing need for more medical research funding, the glaring problems with Prop.
38 make us hesitant to endorse it.
Vote “no” on Prop.
38.

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:

### Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative

### Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026.
To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures.
On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund.
The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive.
